title: Slice-diff investigation protocol and dashboard playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, operational playbook for investigating intermittent or cohort-specific performance regressions using slice-diff comparisons and dashboard-driven triage. It captures a repeatable sequence from alert -> rapid containment -> bisect/profiling -> remediation and follow-up.

Audience and scope:
- Primary: serving runtime engineers and on-call SREs.
- Applies to: latency/throughput regressions surfaced by the performance sentinel, per-route dashboards, or customer reports where the change is not uniform across traffic.
- Not scope: full-scale infra outages, hardware failures, or region-wide network blips (those follow the incident framework).

When to use this protocol:
- Alerts show regression only on a subset of traffic (particular model versions, routes, regions, or token-length bands).
- Canary delta shows a localized p95/p99 spike vs baseline.
- Slowdowns correlate with a recent rollout (model/kernel/quantization change) but root cause is unknown.

Quick triage (first 20 minutes):
1) Record the alert summary and scope in Slack/Ops channel and create a short-lived investigation thread. Capture: alert id, impacted routes/models, delta window, and severity.
2) Pull high-level metrics: p50/p95/p99, request rate, errors, timeouts, CPU/GPU utilization for the span of the delta (15m, 1h, 24h).
   - Dashboards: "Serving: Overview", "Per-route latency map", "Batching & queue depth".
3) Identify hot slices: group by model_version, route, region, instance_type, and input token_count. If the regression is concentrated in one or two cohorts, label them (hot_slice).
4) If regression affects all slices, follow normal incident process. If isolated, continue with slice-diff flow.

Slice-diff concept (short):
- A slice is any dimensioned cohort (example: model=v1.3, route=/chat, region=iad, token_range=256-512).
- Slice-diff compares metric distributions between an impacted slice and a baseline slice (previous stable canary or primary traffic) to focus the investigation on where timing changed.

Essential dashboards and panels to inspect:
- Slice heatmap: p50/p95/p99 by (model_version x region x route). Look for concentrated color bands.
- Token-length latency waterfall: latency vs token_count percentiles. Helpful for spotting tail behavior at longer contexts.
- Batch size / queue depth by slice: to catch batching regressions.
- KV-cache hit ratio + eviction rate per model instance.
- GPU kernels / SM occupancy (if available): sudden drops/increases often map to kernel selection regressions.
- Syscalls and read/write spikes (IO-bound symptoms).
- Canary snapshot compare: side-by-side histograms for baseline vs current (aligned to same slice).

Quick SQL-ish queries (examples to run against the signal store):
- Top offending slices (p95 increase > 30% over baseline):
  SELECT model_version, route, region, token_bucket, p95_delta
  FROM slice_metrics
  WHERE time BETWEEN now()-1h AND now()
    AND p95_delta > 0.3
  ORDER BY p95_delta DESC
  LIMIT 50;

- Token distribution for a slice:
  SELECT token_count, count(1) as n, percentile(latency, 95) as p95
  FROM requests
  WHERE model_version='v1.3' AND route='/chat' AND time BETWEEN start AND end
  GROUP BY token_count
  ORDER BY token_count;

Bisect strategy (if suspect rollout):
1) Canary snapshot compare: pick two snapshots (last known-good vs current) and run a deterministic comparison on identical synthetic prompts. If delta reproduces, continue to code/commit bisect.
2) Commit bisect (narrow to change set): if can reproduce with synthetic harness, do a git bisect across commits between known-good and current deployed model/runtime. Use the bench harness to run microbench (50-200 synthetic runs per commit).
3) Canary traffic bisect (if rolling configs): re-run the canary rollout with binary search on config flags (e.g., quantize=true/false, kernel selection overrides) to isolate flag that flips the behavior.

Profiling steps (non-blocking and blocking):
- Non-blocking: enable additional tracing on a small percentage of traffic for affected slice(s). Capture: callchain duration, kernel selection, batch composition, KV cache event id, and queue wait times.
- Blocking (if reproducible): run on a repro host with profiler tools: Nsight Systems for kernel timelines, per-op timing counters; torch.profiler / Triton traces for op-level; and perf/ebpf for syscalls. Snapshot logs and upload to perf-bucket.
- Look for: sudden new op added to hot path, quantized kernel path differences, fallback to slower codepath (e.g., FP32->FP16 fallback), dramatic increase in queue wait times (backpressure).

Hypotheses checklist (things that commonly cause slice-specific regressions):
- New kernel selection changed at certain sequence lengths.
- KV cache eviction pattern changed (cold-slice misses spike).
- Batching policy or tokenization changes producing different token_count distribution.
- Model quantization artifacts forcing slower fallback.
- Memory pressure -> increased GC or swapping on worker.
- Input distribution changes (longer conversations) leading to longer KV cache lookups.

Containment and short-term mitigations:
- Route pin to previous model_version (roll back routing rule for affected slice).
- Increase instance pool for impacted dedicated capacity to lower queueing and drain backlog.
- Turn off an experimental config flag (quantization_override, new-kernel-opt) for a short window.
- Apply rate-limit to heavy slices while investigating.

Communication template (post to incident/thread):
- One-line summary: what, who, impact (users/traffic %), and mitigation in place.
- Current hypothesis and next action.
- Owners and ETA for next update.

Decision record and follow-up actions (30/60/90 days):
- Keep a short decision log: why we rolled back or accepted the change and the experiments needed to validate the fix.
- Add the offending slice and signature queries to the regression watchlist.
- If change was code/kernel-level: add a perf test in CI that runs the synthetic slice harness at representative token lengths and compares baseline p95/p99.

Template: quick investigation log (paste into the Slack thread)
- Alert ID: <id>
- Time window: <start> - <end>
- Hot slices: model=v1.3, route=/chat, region=iad, token_bucket=256-512 (40% of delta)
- Metrics: p95 +42%, p99 +85%, RPS steady
- Immediate mitigation: rolled route->v1.2 for /chat in iad at 14:12 UTC
- Repro: synthetic harness reproduces +38% p95 when using kernel-build-2025-11-02
- Next steps: commit-bisect starting with PR#2345; egress profiling snapshot captures queued_wait spikes.

Open questions / TODOs (workshop list):
- Should we auto-flag slices with p95 increase and small traffic share (to catch regressions early even if impact is small)?
- Add a standardized snapshot format for canary histograms that includes token_count breakdowns.
- Improve trace sampling to include kernel selection metadata by default.

References and bookmarks:
- Perf bucket: gs://redwood-perf/snapshots/ (use with access request)
- Synthetic harness: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-bench (see /scripts/slice-repro.sh)
- Existing dashboard: Serving / Slice heatmap (linked in artifacts above)

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep this doc short and action-oriented. Make an example incident template that can be copied into postmortems.
- Follow-up: coordinate with product for any customer-facing communication if rollback impacts experiments.
__notes: internal: created as a working playbook, not a final SOP
